title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis
authors: Sikha O K, Abdollah Moslemi, Elham Alizadeh, Ludovic Humbert, Miguel A. Gonzalez Ballester, Jerome Noailly
abstract: Hip fractures represent a significant clinical challenge because they cause excess disability and mortality, and have a growing incidence in aging populations, as bone fragility increases. Although finite element analysis (FEA) provides biomechanical assessment of femoral strength, its clinical applicability is mainly limited by high computational cost. Conventional machine learning (ML) approaches have been explored as surrogate models for FEA; predictions are fast but fail to capture the spatial and topological structure of finite element meshes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based framework for femoral stress prediction using graph-structured finite element modeling (FEM) data. The proposed GCN-SAGE-Residual architecture combines graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning to model spatial dependencies and stress propagation across mesh elements. We systematically evaluated 14 models in a primary comparison, spanning classical ML methods and baseline GNN architectures, complemented by a targeted architectural ablation that isolates the contribution of each component of the proposed design. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid architecture achieves the strongest predictive performance among all evaluated models. The proposed hybrid model achieves the best performance with an R^2 score of 0.8022 and mean absolute error of 2.879 MPa, highlighting the importance of incorporating mesh topology in biomechanical prediction tasks. The proposed framework provides a scalable and computationally efficient alternative for FEM-based orthopedic analyses and fracture risk assessment. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid GCN-SAGE-Residual model predicts element-wise femoral stress while capturing finite element mesh topology.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate offers a computationally efficient alternative to femoral FEA, with potential applications in orthopedic analysis and fracture risk assessment.
method: Represent finite element mesh data as a graph.
Combine graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning.
Learn spatial dependencies and stress propagation across mesh elements.
infographic.evidence_signal: The hybrid model performed best in a 14-model comparison, achieving R² = 0.8022 and MAE = 2.879 MPa; targeted ablations examined architectural contributions.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish generalization to unseen anatomies, loading conditions, or mesh resolutions.
infographic.paper_title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis

title: Frame Based Inelasticity for Strength and Fracture in Anisotropic Media
authors: Robert Lipton, Prakash K. C.
abstract: A field theory is presented for predicting damage and fracture in brittle materials. Four concepts are used: a new nonlocal deformation gradient for dynamic stress analysis in anisotropic media, a new type of phase field coming from a constitutive law, the evolution of material displacement from Newton's second law, and a new incorporation of scaled strength surfaces into constitutive laws for predicting dynamic and quasi-static fracture patterns. The elastic softening is governed by the strain dynamics through the constitutive law and in this way we provide the two way coupling between strain and fracture. Simulations validating the approach for both dynamic and quasi-static fracture analysis are compared to experimental results and other simulation methods. The model is capable of predicting material strength in titania and the competition between strength and energy in soda lime glass and titana and captures dynamic crack branching in soda lime glass and concrete.

infographic.key_insight: A frame-based nonlocal theory couples strain and fracture through constitutive softening to predict strength and crack evolution in anisotropic brittle materials.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports dynamic and quasi-static fracture prediction where material strength, fracture energy, and anisotropy influence failure.
method: Use a nonlocal deformation gradient for dynamic stress analysis.
Derive a phase field from the constitutive law, incorporating scaled strength surfaces.
Evolve displacement with Newton’s second law and couple strain to fracture through elastic softening.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparisons with experiments and other simulation methods, including strength prediction in titania, strength–energy competition in glass and titania, and dynamic crack branching in glass and concrete.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify prediction errors or computational cost, leaving accuracy and scalability to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Frame Based Inelasticity for Strength and Fracture in Anisotropic Media

title: A locking-free enriched linearized neural network for linear elasticity
authors: Bonyong Kim, Young Ju Lee
abstract: Volumetric locking remains a fundamental challenge for neural-network Galerkin methods in nearly incompressible elasticity. We introduce the \emph{locking-free enriched linearized neural network} (LF-ENN), to the best of our knowledge, the first neural-network Galerkin method with a rigorous locking-free guarantee. Building on the enriched Galerkin framework, the method combines neural approximation with a structure-preserving enrichment that reduces the discrete incompressibility constraint to a graph-Laplacian problem. This construction enables divergence-free corrections and error estimates uniform in the Lamé parameter $λ\in(0,\infty]$. Nitsche boundary enforcement and tailored stabilization overcome the lack of conventional finite element trace inequalities for neural trial spaces. Under suitable approximation and mesh-resolution assumptions, we establish stability and error estimates independent of network width, mesh size, and $λ$, including an $O(h^s)$ estimate for reduced-regularity solutions with $s>1/2$. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions confirm locking-free behavior and demonstrate substantial gains in displacement accuracy. In particular, LF-ENN achieves approximately twelve times smaller displacement error than a higher-order locking-free enriched Galerkin method while using fewer than one-third as many unknowns. These results establish a rigorous neural Galerkin framework that combines incompressibility robustness with markedly improved approximation accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: LF-ENN combines neural approximation with structure-preserving enrichment to provide a rigorous locking-free guarantee for nearly incompressible linear elasticity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports accurate displacement prediction near incompressibility without the artificial stiffening caused by volumetric locking.
method: Enrich a linearized neural trial space within an enriched Galerkin framework.
Reduce discrete incompressibility constraints to a graph-Laplacian problem, enabling divergence-free corrections.
Use Nitsche boundary enforcement and tailored stabilization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two- and three-dimensional experiments confirm locking-free behavior; a reported comparison achieves approximately 12× smaller displacement error than a higher-order locking-free enriched Galerkin method using fewer than one-third as many unknowns.
infographic.watch_item: The theoretical guarantees require suitable approximation and mesh-resolution assumptions; fewer unknowns do not alone establish lower computational cost.
infographic.paper_title: A locking-free enriched linearized neural network for linear elasticity

title: Axion: A differentiable, GPU-native finite element framework,demonstrated on phase-field fracture
authors: Wei Wang, Meenu Krishnan U., Somdatta Goswami
abstract: We introduce Axion (Autodifferentiable, XLA-compiled, Implicit, On-device Numerics), a differentiable, GPU-native finite element framework written in JAX. The element kernels, Newton and Krylov iterations, bound-constrained updates, staggered coupling of fields, and the loop over load increments are expressed as a single program that is just-in-time compiled and executed on the GPU without host intervention. Consistent tangent operators are obtained by forward-mode automatic differentiation of the element residual, and derivatives of the discrete solution with respect to model parameters are obtained by differentiating the same program. Global operators are applied element by element without assembling a sparse matrix, octree mesh refinement is performed within fixed-size arrays, and a cell-based domain decomposition runs the same program on several GPUs. Phase-field fracture is implemented as the first module because it combines fine mesh resolution, bound-constrained damage, and repeated nonlinear solves over a loading history, which together make it computationally expensive. On two- and three-dimensional single-edge-notched tension benchmarks, a uniformly refined Axion computation completes faster than the corresponding adaptive FEniCSx computation. At identical discretization, the two-dimensional benchmark runs 37.9 times faster on one GPU than a FEniCSx implementation on one CPU. Strong and weak scaling efficiencies on four GPUs are 92% and 96%, respectively. Large-scale demonstrations include hydraulic fracture in a poroelastic medium (0.38M degrees of freedom), fracture of a multi-material premolar under contact loading (0.69M degrees of freedom), and a concrete gravity dam (96M degrees of freedom) on a single GPU. The implementation is available as open-source software.

infographic.key_insight: Axion makes differentiable phase-field fracture simulation GPU-native by compiling the full finite element solution workflow into one JAX program.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster fracture simulations and parameter sensitivities could support large-scale failure analysis and gradient-based calibration or design.
method: JIT-compiles element kernels, nonlinear solves, damage constraints, and load stepping for execution without host intervention.
Uses automatic differentiation for consistent tangents and solution sensitivities, with matrix-free global operators.
Supports fixed-array octree refinement and multi-GPU cell-based domain decomposition.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a 37.9× speedup over single-CPU FEniCSx at identical 2D discretization, 92% strong and 96% weak scaling efficiency on four GPUs, and a 96M-DOF dam simulation on one GPU.
infographic.watch_item: The headline speedup compares one GPU with one CPU, so it should not be interpreted as a hardware-matched measure of algorithmic advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Axion: A differentiable, GPU-native finite element framework,demonstrated on phase-field fracture

title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
authors: Yuan Qiu, Wolfgang Dahmen, Peng Chen
abstract: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

infographic.key_insight: A variationally correct first-order least-squares residual makes physics-informed operator learning locally reliable by linking training loss to error in the PDE-compliant norm.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, this approach supports finite-element-compatible neural surrogates with a physics-based error indicator at inference.
method: Establish residual–error equivalence using linearized stability and Lipschitz continuity of the residual derivative.
Train a reduced-basis neural operator in a conforming finite element space, using solution snapshots only to construct the basis.
Assemble the residual loss and its symbolically derived gradient with a finite element library.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests show that the square root of loss excess tracks error and that the operator outperforms grid-based baselines in the PDE-compliant norm when evaluated in the same finite element space.
infographic.watch_item: Residual–error guarantees depend on PDE-specific stability and regularity conditions and may hold only near a solution branch.
infographic.paper_title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations

title: Nonlocal regularization of sharp-crack energetics: a variational bridge from Griffith geometry to emergent constitutive degradation
authors: Qing Cheng, Yuqi Sun, Xuejun Xu
abstract: We develop a variational diffuse-crack model based on nonlocal averaging of tensile strain energy. A bounded potential acts on the scaled average, while the compressive energy remains local. The initial slope preserves the averaged tensile strain-energy density to leading order. The first variation yields a constitutive stress in which the tensile contribution is multiplied by the adjoint average of the derivative of the saturation potential. The resulting degradation is therefore determined by the stored-energy functional, without introducing an independent fracture field or prescribing a separate degradation law. For fixed smooth displacement fields with bounded strain, the energy density converges to the classical elastic strain-energy density as the averaging radius tends to zero. The Griffith surface-energy coefficient is recovered for planar opening transitions. A structure-preserving scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) scheme satisfies an exact discrete balance between the modified-energy increment and external work. We compare SAV and velocity-Verlet solutions for dynamic crack branching and Kalthoff--Winkler impact.

infographic.key_insight: Nonlocal averaging of tensile strain energy produces constitutive degradation directly from a variational energy functional, without an independent fracture field or prescribed degradation law.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation offers an energy-based route to simulating dynamic brittle fracture while linking diffuse crack behavior to Griffith surface energy.
method: Apply a bounded saturation potential to scaled, nonlocally averaged tensile energy while keeping compressive energy local.
Derive tensile stress degradation through the adjoint averaging operator and the potential derivative.
Use a scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) scheme with an exact discrete modified-energy–work balance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports elastic-limit convergence for fixed smooth, bounded-strain displacements, Griffith coefficient recovery for planar opening transitions, and SAV versus velocity-Verlet comparisons for dynamic branching and Kalthoff–Winkler impact.
infographic.watch_item: The stated elastic-limit and planar-opening results do not establish general Griffith convergence for arbitrary evolving crack geometries.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlocal regularization of sharp-crack energetics: a variational bridge from Griffith geometry to emergent constitutive degradation

title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs
authors: Stanislas Pamela, Nicolas Pailliez, Emmanuel Franck, Victor Michel-Dansac, Laurent Navoret, Vignesh Gopakumar
abstract: Research in the domain of Physics-Informed Neural Networks applied to PDE modelling has advanced significantly in recent years, providing a wide ecosystem of novel methods. However, one frequent limitation is the inability of PINNs to scale out on High-Performance Computing architectures to address more ambitious challenges, particularly non-linear physics models with turbulent dynamics in large spatial domains. Typical studies restrain demonstrations to toy models with simple physics equations, few variables, and rarely any complex non-linear dynamics evolved over long timescales. Part of the AI community has even adopted the idea that "PINNs don't scale". This work proves otherwise. We present a mathematically robust formulation of Finite-Element-Method for Neural Networks (FEM-NN) implemented into a comprehensive, modular framework: Fuse-PINN. This formulation provides the basis for a sclable parallelisation of Physics-Informed Neural Networks on GPU-based HPC systems. Furthermore, an Energy Natural Gradient Descent optimiser is implemented to allow high-precision convergence. Fuse-PINN is demonstrated on physics models relevant to Magnetic Confinement Fusion, including non-linear convective models with fine-scale dynamics. Near-perfect scaling is achieved on multi-GPU runs with increasing problem size.

infographic.key_insight: Fuse-PINN combines finite-element methods and neural networks to enable scalable multi-GPU simulations of nonlinear PDEs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a route to parallel physics-informed simulation of complex nonlinear systems, demonstrated on models relevant to magnetic confinement fusion rather than solid mechanics.
method: Formulates a mathematically grounded Finite-Element-Method for Neural Networks (FEM-NN).
Implements modular GPU-based parallelisation in Fuse-PINN.
Uses Energy Natural Gradient Descent for high-precision convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports near-perfect scaling on multi-GPU runs as problem size increases, with demonstrations including nonlinear convective models exhibiting fine-scale dynamics.
infographic.watch_item: Scaling is reported for increasing problem sizes; fixed-size scaling, hardware requirements, and performance against conventional FEM solvers are not specified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs

title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
authors: Yue Yu, Jihong Wang, Stewart Silling, Ziwei Yang
abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

infographic.key_insight: Mesoscale neural operators learn nonlocal constitutive laws from molecular dynamics while preserving strain energy density and fracture energy under changes in interaction scale.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The learned model enables continuum fracture predictions on domains far larger than atomistic simulations can practically resolve.
method: Learn a nonlocal kernel and nonlinear constitutive relation from MD loading and displacement data.
Normalize the kernel to preserve strain energy density under horizon rescaling.
Rescale critical bond stretch to maintain a consistent energy release rate across scales.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic tests recovered the underlying nonlocal model; MD-based tests matched energy metrics within 3% and out-of-distribution peak forces within 6%, while a plate with 4,000× the training-specimen area exhibited branching fracture.
infographic.watch_item: The reported tests do not establish generalization to other materials or fracture regimes, so application-specific validation remains necessary.
infographic.paper_title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions

title: Locking-free numerical methods for poroelasticity optimal control problems with minimal regularities
authors: Jeonghun J. Lee
abstract: We study distributed optimal control of a linear poroelastic system in a total pressure formulation, with displacement and fluid-pressure tracking and box constraints on the source control. A mechanical Schur complement gives well-posedness at zero storage for each fixed finite Lamé parameter, without estimates that grow like the inverse storage coefficient. We discretize the state and adjoint with conforming finite elements and dG(0) time stepping, and use piecewise constant controls. Under the stated regularity assumptions and a positive lower bound on storage, we prove first-order control and state error estimates uniform as the Lamé parameter increases. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates, examine the dependence on the Lamé and storage coefficients, and demonstrate localized pressure control with active bounds.

infographic.key_insight: A total-pressure formulation enables locking-free poroelastic optimal control, with first-order error estimates uniform as the Lamé parameter increases under stated regularity and positive-storage assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports reliable source-control optimization in nearly incompressible porous materials while enforcing bounds on control inputs.
method: Track displacement and fluid pressure with box-constrained distributed source control.
Use a mechanical Schur complement to establish zero-storage well-posedness for each fixed finite Lamé parameter.
Discretize states and adjoints with conforming finite elements and dG(0) time stepping, using piecewise constant controls.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments confirm predicted convergence rates, examine Lamé-parameter and storage-coefficient dependence, and demonstrate localized pressure control with active bounds.
infographic.watch_item: Zero-storage well-posedness does not imply zero-storage error guarantees: the first-order estimates require a positive lower bound on storage.
infographic.paper_title: Locking-free numerical methods for poroelasticity optimal control problems with minimal regularities

title: From dynamic strain aging to Alessandro--Beatrice--Bertotti--Montorsi dynamics of propagating Portevin--Le Chatelier bands
authors: Tero Mäkinen, Mikko J. Alava
abstract: Type-A Portevin--Le Chatelier bands are propagating strain localizations whose velocity exhibits strong intermittent fluctuations. We derive a coarse-grained connection between the dynamic-strain-aging model of Hähner and Rizzi and the Alessandro--Beatrice--Bertotti--Montorsi (ABBM) mean-field model of avalanche dynamics. A propagating band is reduced to a single phase coordinate while retaining the elastic feedback of the tensile machine. This feedback generates the increasing drive and restoring terms of the ABBM description. A finite-time adjoint calculation determines the stress mobility of the band and is checked independently by direct stress continuation. The mobility is approximately proportional to the hardening parameter, whereas the band speed scales approximately as its square root. Short-range heterogeneity in the plastic strain deposited by the band is converted by the global machine feedback into a Brownian effective force. The resulting reduction provides a microscopic route from dynamic strain aging to ABBM-like avalanche dynamics of propagating PLC bands.

infographic.key_insight: A coarse-grained reduction connects dynamic strain aging in propagating Portevin–Le Chatelier bands to ABBM avalanche dynamics through tensile-machine feedback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework links intermittent plastic-band motion to material hardening and machine feedback, helping interpret unstable deformation during tensile loading.
method: Reduce a propagating band to one phase coordinate while retaining elastic machine feedback.
Compute band stress mobility with a finite-time adjoint and check it by direct stress continuation.
Map short-range fluctuations in deposited plastic strain to a Brownian effective force through global feedback.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports agreement between adjoint and stress-continuation mobility estimates, with mobility approximately proportional to hardening and band speed scaling approximately as its square root.
infographic.watch_item: The reduction targets propagating type-A bands; applicability to other PLC regimes or experimental conditions is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: From dynamic strain aging to Alessandro--Beatrice--Bertotti--Montorsi dynamics of propagating Portevin--Le Chatelier bands

title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers
authors: Jinjun Peng, Wailiang Zhao, Baishakhi Ray, Zhou Yu, Jufeng Yang
abstract: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.

infographic.key_insight: Transformer plasticity and stability depend differently on module function: QK/VO projections learn procedures most readily, while MLPs excel at declarative memorization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Module-targeted updates could help engineering AI systems acquire new procedures while preserving stored knowledge, though solid-mechanics applications were not evaluated.
method: Separate procedural learning from declarative memorization in controlled synthetic tasks.
Compare plasticity and stability across QK, VO, and MLP modules.
Use targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments to probe functional dependencies.
infographic.evidence_signal: During new-procedure learning, QK updates retain over half of stored declarative memory, MLP updates retain far less, and VO updates lose roughly four-fifths; realistic-model experiments broadly echo these asymmetries.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no solid-mechanics validation, so transfer to constitutive modeling remains unproven.
infographic.paper_title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers

title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis
authors: Erfan Hamdi, Joel Shor, Emma Lejeune
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential route to automating scientific programming, but their usefulness depends on consistently producing numerically correct code. We extend FEM-Bench to 17 finite element tasks involving nonlinear and history-dependent mechanics and structural dynamics, and evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation without execution feedback. The best model succeeds in 87.1% of single-pass implementation trials, but rankings differ between tracks. The leading implementer achieves 49.9% joint test success, while the leading tester reaches 82.6%. For six models, we compare single-pass generation with two agentic harnesses that allow code execution and revision. Agentic execution solves some tasks that never succeeded in single-pass trials and improves consistency on others, but gains vary across models and harnesses, and regressions also occur. Claude Opus 5 with SimpleAgent reaches 96.5% Pass@3, the probability of at least one success in three attempts, but 77.1% Pass$^3$, the probability that all three succeed. No model-harness combination exceeds 78.8% Pass$^3$. To understand why agents submit incorrect code after passing their own checks, we analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and identify six categories of self-verification failure. The most common are inadequate test coverage (73.1%) and reliance on generic consistency checks (70.3%), and in 28.5% of cases the tests share an error with the implementation. Motivated by these findings, an exploratory configuration with separate coder and tester agents achieves the highest observed scores, with 97.6% Pass@3 and 88.8% Pass$^3$. These results identify consistency across attempts and independent verification as the main obstacles to trusting LLM-generated scientific code.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs can generate correct finite element code, but inconsistent results and weak self-verification limit trust; separating coder and tester agents shows promise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automating mechanics code requires independent numerical validation, not just passing an agent’s own checks.
method: Extend FEM-Bench to 17 tasks covering nonlinear mechanics, history dependence, and structural dynamics.
Evaluate 15 models on single-pass implementation and test generation, then compare two execution-enabled agentic harnesses for six models.
Analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and explore separate coder and tester agents.
infographic.evidence_signal: The exploratory coder–tester configuration achieved 97.6% probability of at least one success in three attempts and 88.8% probability that all three succeed, versus at most 78.8% all-three success across the primary model–harness comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: Agentic revision can regress performance, and the exploratory coder–tester gains need broader validation before deployment in engineering workflows.
infographic.paper_title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis

title: Differentiable High-Order Mesh $r$-Adaptivity
authors: Ketan Mittal, Julian Andrej, John Camier, Veselin Dobrev, Tzanio Kolev, Leonardo Molinari
abstract: High-order mesh r-adaptivity typically entails minimizing a nonlinear functional using its gradients and, for Newton-based methods, its Hessian. These derivatives can be expensive to derive, must be updated with any changes to the functional, and errors in the derivatives directly impact the convergence of r-adaptivity. Additionally, derivatives of the r-adaptivity operator are required for consistent sensitivity analysis for inverse problems. This work develops a framework for differentiable r-adaptivity based on the Target-Matrix Optimization Paradigm. Given a pointwise functional defining the local mesh-adaptation objective, the proposed framework uses $\partial$FEM to automatically generate pointwise first- and second-order derivatives. These local derivatives are then assembled into a global gradient vector and a Hessian operator through the finite element operator decomposition. The derivative kernels support portable CPU and GPU execution, with partial assembly and tensor sum factorization enabling matrix-free application of the Hessian operator. The framework also provides consistent sensitivities of the r-adaptivity operator through automatically generated mixed derivatives and implicit differentiation of the mesh stationarity equations. Numerical experiments show GPU solve times comparable to those of hand-derived TMOP implementations on a benchmark problem, improvement in r-adaptivity convergence due to accurate computation of the derivatives, and demonstrate the use of mesh sensitivities for material-interface identification in an inverse heat-conduction problem.

infographic.key_insight: Automatically generated derivatives enable differentiable high-order mesh r-adaptivity with accurate optimization gradients, Hessians, and mesh sensitivities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports mesh optimization and consistent sensitivity analysis for inverse engineering problems while reducing manual derivative development.
method: Define local mesh-quality objectives using the Target-Matrix Optimization Paradigm.
Use ∂FEM to generate pointwise first-, second-, and mixed-order derivatives.
Apply finite element operator decomposition for CPU/GPU execution, matrix-free Hessians, and implicit mesh sensitivities.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments report GPU solve times comparable to hand-derived TMOP on a benchmark, improved adaptation convergence, and material-interface identification in an inverse heat-conduction problem.
infographic.watch_item: Consistent implicit mesh sensitivities depend on sufficiently converged stationarity equations and a well-conditioned mesh Hessian.
infographic.paper_title: Differentiable High-Order Mesh $r$-Adaptivity

title: Modelling the human-exoskeleton interaction interface - Benchmarking MuJoCo's deformable model
authors: Lisette Masselink, Xiaolong Zhu Thomas George Thuruthel, Mohamed Irfan Refai
abstract: The human-exoskeleton interaction interface, consisting of the exoskeleton attachment and the underlying human soft tissue, can affect the transfer of assistance. MuJoCo's \textit{flexcomp} has been previously used to model the soft tissue, but its accuracy has not been benchmarked against a finite element model. We benchmarked the \textit{flexcomp} Saint Venant-Kirchhoff (StVK) and Stable Neo-Hookean (SNH) models against COMSOL's Yeoh model in three cases: \textit{case 1}) spherical indentation, \textit{case 2}) compression, and \textit{case 3}) compression of a thigh. We compared force and strain energy as a function of indentation depth, hysteresis and computation time. MuJoCo's models capture force trends with a correlation of 0.97-0.99, but showed a stiffer response, which could be attributed to the volumetric locking of the linear finite elements. The MuJoCo models systematically underestimated hysteresis as MuJoCo's Rayleigh damping could not substitute a viscoelastic model. Moreover, MuJoCo's computational advantage was speed dependent: it was 2-2.5 times faster for spherical indentation, but COMSOL was faster for the other cases, which have more degrees of freedom and contacts. Although MuJoCo's \textit{flexcomp} offers a combination of soft-tissue modelling and multibody dynamics, the limitations regarding the stiffening and hysteresis should be addressed to be used for the analysis of the human-exoskeleton interaction interface.

infographic.key_insight: MuJoCo’s deformable models tracked reference force trends closely but were too stiff and underestimated hysteresis, limiting their accuracy for human–exoskeleton interfaces.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Soft-tissue model choice can affect predictions of how exoskeleton attachments transfer assistance to the body.
method: Benchmarked MuJoCo flexcomp Saint Venant–Kirchhoff and Stable Neo-Hookean models against COMSOL’s Yeoh model.
Tested spherical indentation, compression, and thigh compression.
Compared force and strain energy versus indentation depth, hysteresis, and computation time.
infographic.evidence_signal: Force correlations were 0.97–0.99; MuJoCo was 2–2.5× faster for spherical indentation, but COMSOL was faster in the other two cases.
infographic.watch_item: Possible volumetric locking may explain excess stiffness, while Rayleigh damping did not reproduce viscoelastic hysteresis.
infographic.paper_title: Modelling the human-exoskeleton interaction interface - Benchmarking MuJoCo's deformable model

title: A Staggered Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Network Method with a Computable Error Decomposition
authors: Gung-Min Gie, Chang-Yeol Jung, Bongsuk Kwon, Kiwoong Kwon
abstract: We develop a staggered discontinuous Galerkin neural network (SDGNN) method for scalar elliptic problems with a computable error decomposition. The staggered discontinuous Galerkin (SDG) method requires only local continuity of its trial functions and gives a square, inf-sup stable system without stabilization parameters; we carry this structure over to neural networks. Networks defined on the patches of a staggered mesh satisfy the SDG continuity conditions for all values of the network parameters, and the loss is the squared dual norm of the SDG weak residual. We show that the loss is equivalent, with computable constants, to the square of the training error, the distance between the SDG projection of the network and the SDG finite element approximation, so that the full error is bounded by the discretization error, a multiple of the square root of the loss, and the network projection error. The weak residual requires no derivatives of the networks, the boundary and convection terms carry no penalty or stabilization weights, and the scalar trial functions may jump across the midlines of the primal cells. Numerical experiments show that the square root of the loss tracks the error during the training, that prescribed jumps across a square and a circular interface are captured consistently over the initializations, and that the method is more accurate than physics-informed neural networks at the same parameter counts.

infographic.key_insight: SDGNN preserves staggered discontinuous Galerkin structure while providing a computable error bound separating discretization, training, and network projection errors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers an error-monitorable neural solver for scalar elliptic engineering models, including problems with prescribed interface jumps.
method: Define patchwise networks that satisfy SDG continuity conditions for every parameter choice.
Train using the squared dual norm of the SDG weak residual, without network derivatives or penalty and stabilization weights.
Relate loss to training error through computable constants and bound total error using three components.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments report that square-root loss tracks error during training, prescribed square and circular interface jumps are captured consistently across initializations, and accuracy exceeds PINNs at equal parameter counts.
infographic.watch_item: The loss controls training error, not total error by itself; discretization and network projection errors must also be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: A Staggered Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Network Method with a Computable Error Decomposition

title: A mesoscale damage model for void nucleation and growth in shock loaded microstructure informed by computer vision
authors: Abhijith Thoopul Anantharanga, Brandon Runnels
abstract: Spallation in ductile materials under high strain rates occurs through the process of void nucleation, growth, and coalescence. Void nucleation is known to depend on factors ranging from microstructural to stress state. The criteria for void nucleation in damage models are stochastic, and microstructural awareness is often neglected. Recently, it was shown that nucleation propensity can be estimated using computer vision. In the present work, this is integrated with a continuum damage model framework for comprehensive simulation of spallation in tantalum under plate impact. Void nucleation probability is governed by a susceptibility field, predicted from grain orientations and grain boundary (GB) energy, with a mechanical barrier set by the local maximum principal stress. This is coupled to a crystal plasticity model within a Lagrangian shock simulation, with microstructure selectively resolved to reduce computational cost. The model is calibrated at a flyer velocity of 196 m/s, where the simulated free surface velocity (FSV) matches experimental measurements of shock arrival, peak state, release and the pullback signal measured in flyer impact experiments, with some deviations confined to the late time ringing. With no further parameter changes, the model transfers to a 214 m/s case and accurately reproduces the FSV. To demonstrate the microstructure-awareness of the nucleation model, a selection of synthetic microstructures is presented for comparison. In the resolved microstructure, voids nucleate predominantly (though not exclusively) at GBs and triple junctions. It is shown that the FSV differs significantly based on the incorporated microstructure, yielding the correct FSV prediction only in the case of representative microstructures.

infographic.key_insight: Computer-vision-informed void nucleation makes shock damage predictions sensitive to microstructure, with representative microstructures needed to reproduce measured free-surface velocity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model supports microstructure-aware prediction of spallation in shock-loaded tantalum while selectively resolving microstructure to limit computational cost.
method: Predict a void-nucleation susceptibility field from grain orientations and grain-boundary energy using computer vision.
Combine susceptibility with a local maximum-principal-stress barrier in a continuum damage model.
Couple damage to crystal plasticity within a Lagrangian shock simulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calibrated at a flyer velocity of 196 m/s, the model matched major experimental free-surface-velocity features and reproduced a 214 m/s case without further parameter changes.
infographic.watch_item: Predictions depend on representative microstructure inputs, and deviations remain in late-time ringing.
infographic.paper_title: A mesoscale damage model for void nucleation and growth in shock loaded microstructure informed by computer vision

title: PANO: Parallel Latent Space Neural Operator for Solving PDEs
authors: Zijiang Yang, Xiaomeng Wu, Chen Kuang, Dongmei Fu
abstract: Aggregating observations into a limited number of latent tokens and learning physical interactions in the latent space has emerged as an effective approach for Transformer-based neural operators to solve Partial Differential Equation (PDE) problems involving large-scale observations. However, existing methods typically compress observations using a single aggregation pattern, making physical information not retained by that pattern invisible to the latent space and thereby constraining physical interactions within it. To address this limitation, we propose PArallel Latent Space Neural Operator (PANO), a novel neural operator for solving PDEs that formulates physical interactions among observations as an additive combination of interaction results from parallel latent spaces with shared parameters. Specifically, PANO transforms observations into multiple distinct compressed representations through independent mappings, learns physical interactions in parallel based on these representations, and finally fuses the decoded results to predict the target physical field. Within PANO, we further propose Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) to construct bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding mappings, and Pairwise Latent Space Attention Layer (PaLA) to jointly update latent representations of each latent space through adaptive cross-space interactions. Extensive experiments on nine benchmarks spanning diverse physical systems, geometries, and observation scales demonstrate that PANO achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, PANO reduces equivalent plastic strain prediction errors on Unilateral Stamping by 28.3% (or more) and lift-coefficient prediction errors on AirCraft by 21.4% (or more) compared with existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/ZijiangY1116/PANO.

infographic.key_insight: PANO combines interactions learned in parallel latent spaces to retain physical information that a single compression pattern may miss.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports PDE surrogates for mechanics applications, including equivalent plastic strain prediction in stamping and aerodynamic lift prediction.
method: Compress observations into distinct latent representations through independent mappings, with shared parameters for interaction learning.
Use Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) for bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding mappings.
Use Pairwise Latent Space Attention (PaLA) for adaptive cross-space interactions, then fuse decoded outputs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across nine benchmarks covering diverse physical systems, geometries, and observation scales, the abstract reports state-of-the-art performance, including error reductions of at least 28.3% for Unilateral Stamping strain and 21.4% for AirCraft lift coefficient versus existing methods.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify computational overhead or establish reliability outside the tested benchmarks, both important for engineering deployment.
infographic.paper_title: PANO: Parallel Latent Space Neural Operator for Solving PDEs

title: Pharmaco-mechanical computational simulation of atherosclerotic arteries: effects of calcium channel blockers on local stress distributions
authors: Sharan Nurani Ramesh, Lea Saßmannshausen, Axel Klawonn, Daniel Balzani
abstract: This paper presents a computational model integrating transmural drug transport, smooth muscle cell contraction, nonlinear anisotropic material behavior, and residual stresses to investigate the effects of calcium channel blockers~(CCBs) on local stress distributions in atherosclerotic arteries. The balance of linear momentum is coupled with a three-dimensional reaction-diffusion equation for the drug transport. Smooth muscle contraction is modeled phenomenologically based on a chemo-mechanical model that incorporates the effects of stretch on intracellular calcium dynamics and calcium sensitization. A novel drug-tissue interaction model is proposed to capture the effects of CCBs on intracellular calcium and thus on smooth muscle contraction. Material parameters are identified by fitting to experimental data from the literature and finite element simulations are conducted on five exemplary atherosclerotic arterial geometries reconstructed from histological cross-sections. Simulation results show that although CCBs reduce the stresses in the media through reduced smooth muscle contraction, they shift load to the fibrous cap, whose stress increases in all five geometries (median of up to 28.9~kPa). This increase varies strongly between plaque morphologies and becomes smaller with lower smooth muscle tone before treatment, lower drug concentrations in the arterial wall and increasing axial pre-stretch. A blood pressure reduction of 10~mmHg already lowers it to a median of at most 3.8~kPa in four of the five geometries. Our findings suggest that CCBs may increase the rupture risk of vulnerable plaques with highly loaded fibrous caps under insufficient blood pressure reduction, which remains to be confirmed experimentally and clinically.

infographic.key_insight: Calcium channel blockers reduce arterial media stress but can shift load to the fibrous cap, potentially increasing plaque rupture risk if blood pressure is insufficiently reduced.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coupled drug-transport and arterial-mechanics simulations can reveal local stress changes that may be missed when assessing treatment through blood pressure alone.
method: Couple 3D reaction–diffusion drug transport with finite element arterial mechanics.
Model calcium-dependent smooth muscle contraction, nonlinear anisotropic tissue behavior, and residual stresses.
Fit material parameters to published experiments and simulate five histology-derived atherosclerotic geometries.
infographic.evidence_signal: Fibrous-cap stress increased in all five geometries, with median increases up to 28.9 kPa; a 10 mmHg blood pressure reduction limited median increases to at most 3.8 kPa in four geometries.
infographic.watch_item: Predicted rupture-risk implications require experimental and clinical confirmation; the study evaluates only five exemplary geometries.
infographic.paper_title: Pharmaco-mechanical computational simulation of atherosclerotic arteries: effects of calcium channel blockers on local stress distributions

title: Semi-Implicit and Convex Splitting Schemes for the Surface Cahn--Hilliard Equation on Curved Closed Surfaces
authors: Harri Hakula, Antti Rasila, Xinpeng Xu
abstract: The surface Cahn--Hilliard equation describes phase separation and coarsening of a conserved composition field on fixed curved surfaces. We study a mixed $hp$-surface finite element discretization with curvilinear high-order elements, primarily on the sphere, with the stabilized semi-implicit BDF2 integrator and a stabilized convex-splitting variant solved with the same factorization. For the semi-implicit scheme with a quadratic-growth potential and a truncated nonlinear bulk chemical-potential term, we prove exact discrete mass conservation, energy decay for the start-up steps, an exact per-step energy balance for the BDF2 phase, and a conditional monotone law for a modified Lyapunov functional. A manufactured solution with analytic forcing verifies second order in time and the expected $h$- and $p$-convergence. Torus tests include controlled equal-area bands, whose diffuse energies reproduce sharp-interface perimeters within $1\%$, deterministic coarsening, and a viscous R{ä}tz--Voigt model. Genus-two and genus-three calculations on implicit surfaces conserve mass to roundoff, and their unstable-mode counts agree with area-based Weyl estimates within $1\%$.

infographic.key_insight: High-order surface finite elements paired with stabilized time integrators model conserved phase separation on curved closed surfaces while providing discrete mass and energy guarantees.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports accurate simulation of composition evolution on curved interfaces where geometry, conservation, and numerical stability matter.
method: Mixed hp-surface finite elements with curvilinear high-order geometry.
Stabilized semi-implicit BDF2 and convex-splitting variants using the same factorization.
Discrete analysis of mass conservation, energy balance, and conditional modified-energy decay.
infographic.evidence_signal: Manufactured solutions verify second-order time accuracy and expected h/p convergence; torus interface energies and higher-genus unstable-mode counts match reference estimates within 1%, with higher-genus mass conserved to roundoff.
infographic.watch_item: The semi-implicit energy guarantees require the stated potential and nonlinear truncation assumptions, and modified-energy monotonicity is conditional.
infographic.paper_title: Semi-Implicit and Convex Splitting Schemes for the Surface Cahn--Hilliard Equation on Curved Closed Surfaces

title: On global error estimates of a local discontinuous Galerkin method of the Boussinesq system of equations
authors: Debendra K. Swain, Saumya Bajpai, Deepjyoti Goswami
abstract: In this paper, we develop and analyze a local discontinuous Galerkin (LDG) finite element method for the Boussinesq system of equations, and employ an upwind scheme to effectively manage the nonlinear convective terms, thereby ensuring stability and accuracy. Our analysis establishes new \emph{a priori} regularity estimates for the semidiscrete LDG approximations. We establish optimal \emph{a priori} error estimates for the velocity approximation in $\bL^2$--norm, the pressure approximation in $L^2$--norm and for temperature in $L^2$--norm for all $t>0$. Our proof relies on the standard elliptic and parabolic duality arguments and modified Stokes operators defined on appropriate broken Sobolev spaces. Under suitable smallness assumptions on the given data, we further establish error estimates that remain uniform in time. Furthermore, the backward Euler scheme is considered for a full discretization, and optimal fully discrete error estimates are derived. Finally, we carry out numerical experiments to substantiate our theoretical findings.

infographic.key_insight: An upwind local discontinuous Galerkin method achieves optimal error estimates for Boussinesq velocity, pressure, and temperature, with time-uniform bounds under suitable small-data assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The analysis supports reliable finite element simulation of buoyancy-driven flows and coupled heat transport.
method: Use LDG spatial discretization with upwind treatment of nonlinear convection.
Establish regularity and error bounds using elliptic/parabolic duality and modified Stokes operators.
Apply backward Euler time stepping and derive optimal fully discrete error estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments substantiate the theoretical findings, but the abstract provides no benchmark details or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Time-uniform error guarantees require suitable smallness assumptions on the input data.
infographic.paper_title: On global error estimates of a local discontinuous Galerkin method of the Boussinesq system of equations
